# Nutrition plan — moderate fat loss alongside a return to running

*Fictional illustration of [`templates/nutrition-plan.md`](../../templates/nutrition-plan.md). Not a
plan for any real person, and not guidance to anyone. Every value below is invented for the
illustration and marked accordingly.*

Sixteen weeks, alongside the training in [`fitness-plan.md`](fitness-plan.md).

## Targets

| | Target | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Energy | 2,150 kcal/day (estimated) | Estimated maintenance minus a moderate deficit. Maintenance itself is an estimate from a prediction equation plus activity, and carries substantial individual error |
| Protein | 130 g/day (estimated) | Set from body mass and raised for the deficit and the resistance training, both of which increase requirements |
| Fiber | 30 g/day (estimated) | Toward general recommendations, and a practical proxy for overall dietary quality |

**Rate of change.** Expect somewhere in the region of 0.3–0.6 kg per week, most likely toward the
lower end as the deficit's relative size grows. That is a range rather than a figure, and it is wide
because the response to a given intake varies with body composition, adaptation, adherence, and
measurement error.

**What will be watched instead of a promise:** the four-week rolling average of morning body weight,
and whether training quality is holding. If the average has not moved over four weeks, that is a
decision point — see Review.

**A note on the deficit's size.** It is deliberately moderate rather than aggressive, because this
plan runs alongside a return to running. A larger deficit would compromise the training this plan
exists to support, and a plan that undermines its own leading goal has not made a trade-off, it has
made a mistake ([Standard 39](../../standards/39-goal-compatibility.md)).

## Adequacy

**Nutrients this plan's structure puts at risk:**

- **Protein**, because it is the thing most easily displaced when a calorie target is the focus. It
  is a stated target here rather than a residual for exactly that reason, and it is what — together
  with the resistance training — keeps the weight lost from being disproportionately muscle.
- **Iron**, given the running. Endurance training raises requirements, and this is a nutrient where
  intake and status frequently diverge.
- **Calcium and vitamin D**, given the impact loading and the deficit — bone is adapting to running
  during a period of reduced intake.
- **Fibre and micronutrients generally**, since a deficit means less total food and therefore less
  room for everything.

**How they are covered:** protein and fibre are explicit daily targets. Iron, calcium, and vitamin D
are addressed through the food pattern in Approach rather than by supplementation.

**Not addressed here:** whether this person's actual status for any of these is adequate. That is a
question for testing, not for inference from a diet plan — attributing symptoms to a specific
deficiency from dietary patterns would be inference presented as a finding
([Standard 36](../../standards/36-micronutrient-adequacy.md) R6). If there is reason to suspect one,
that is a conversation with a GP.

## Restrictions and Context

**Safety-critical:** none known.

**Medical:** none known. No medications reported.

**Ethical or religious:** none reported.

**Intolerance and preference:** dislikes most fish, which is relevant to how the iron and omega-3
sides of the pattern are built.

**Practical:** cooks most evenings, eats lunch at work four days a week, moderate budget, no
constraint on time for breakfast. Shares evening meals with a household of three, so evening meals
have to work for everyone — this is a real constraint on the plan and not a preference to be
optimised away.

**Cultural:** no specific pattern reported.

Where any of this is wrong or has changed, it changes the plan rather than the person's adherence
being at fault.

## Approach

Built around the household's existing evening meals with protein raised, rather than a separate set
of meals that would need cooking twice. A plan requiring two dinners is a plan that lasts about three
weeks.

- **Breakfast and lunch** carry most of the protein target, since evening meals are shared and less
  adjustable.
- **Legumes, whole grains, and vegetables** across the day carry the fibre target and most of the
  iron and micronutrient contribution, given the dislike of fish.
- **No food is excluded.** There is no reason to exclude anything here — there is no allergy, no
  condition, and no evidence that would justify it. Restriction adopted without a proportionate
  reason tends to persist past any benefit and to expand.
- **The birthday cake at work is fine.** So is the meal out. A pattern across sixteen weeks is what
  determines the outcome; a single meal is not a meaningful part of it, and treating it as one is how
  people abandon plans that were working.

**On language:** foods here are described by what they contribute. Nothing in this plan is clean,
dirty, a cheat, or earned. That is not squeamishness — shame predicts concealment and abandonment
rather than adherence, and it makes this plan less likely to work.

**If adherence slips**, the first thing to examine is this plan: whether it needs more time or effort
than is available, whether the protein target is realistic given the shared meals, whether the
deficit is too large alongside the training.

## Review

**Every four weeks**, aligned with the training plan's review.

**Body weight** is read as a four-week rolling average, not as individual mornings. Day to day it
moves on water, glycogen, sodium, gut contents, and cycle — routinely by more than a week of actual
fat change. Early loss will overstate fat loss, and starting the running may produce an apparent
stall or gain from glycogen and fluid that is not a stall at all.

**Also assessed:** whether training quality is holding, whether energy is adequate through the day,
whether the protein target is actually being met rather than merely stated, and whether the plan
still fits the household's week.

**When the rate slows** — and it will, as body mass falls and expenditure with it — that is a
decision point with three options: adjust intake, adjust activity, or accept the slower rate. It is
explicitly *not* an automatic reason to cut further. Cutting further at each slowdown is how a
moderate plan becomes a crash diet one step at a time, and no single step in that sequence looks like
the moment it went wrong.
